analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance program covering every American, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and private plans.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 62 cosponsors—61 Democrats and 1 Independent—but was never considered by any of the four committees it was sent to, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have created a national health program run by the states under federal standards, giving every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident comprehensive health coverage with no deductibles or copays for most care. It would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, federal employee health benefits, and military civilian health benefits, and would have banned the sale of private health insurance that duplicates the public coverage. The program would be financed by a new payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, and higher tobacco taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident alien would be automatically enrolled in a State health security program covering hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, long-term care, preventive services, and more, with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copays for acute and preventive care [S2][S3]. Families currently paying premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket costs would stop paying them; the uninsured would gain full coverage; people would keep their coverage when changing jobs or states [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a universal entitlement: every resident who is a citizen, national, or lawful resident alien is entitled to health benefits through a State health security program, enrolled automatically at birth, at immigration, or on January 1, 2007 [S3].

Coverage is comprehensive—hospital care, professional services, prescription drugs, dental, mental health and substance abuse treatment, nursing facility and home-based long-term care, preventive services including eyeglasses and hearing aids—with no deductibles, coinsurance, or copayments for acute and preventive care [S3].
Benefits are portable across state lines, and no provider may balance-bill patients for covered services, ending surprise medical charges [S3].
Long-term care cost-sharing (20% for home and community-based services, 35% for nursing facilities) is waived or reduced for people near the poverty line [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The program is financed through a new payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, and increased excise taxes on tobacco products, deposited in an American Health Security Trust Fund [S2][S3]. Employers would pay the new payroll tax, though many would shed the private insurance premiums they pay today. Tobacco users would pay higher excise taxes. The health insurance industry's core business would be eliminated: the bill bans the sale of any health insurance that duplicates the public program's benefits [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill raises taxes substantially—a new employer payroll tax, a health care income tax, and higher tobacco excise taxes—to fund the program, and opponents argued the cost and the national health security budget would grow beyond projections [S2][S3].

The transition is abrupt: Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, Federal Employees Health Benefits, and CHAMPUS benefits all end after December 31, 2006, private duplicative insurance is banned, and employers, insurers, and states would have to rebuild how coverage is financed and delivered on a fixed deadline [S3].

Not everything is free: home and community-based long-term care carries 20% coinsurance and nursing facility care 35%, with waivers only for those near poverty, and mental health inpatient and residential services have day limits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most households the trade is straightforward: private premiums, deductibles, and copays disappear in exchange for higher taxes, and everyone—including the roughly uninsured—gets coverage they can't lose. The serious honest concerns are the scale of the financing shift onto employers and taxpayers, the abrupt termination of existing programs on a single deadline, and the risk that a single-payer system under global hospital budgets could constrain access or innovation in ways the bill's safeguards only partly address. The bill was an aspirational single-payer proposal written without bipartisan input, which shows in its all-at-once transition design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees, then to two subcommittees, and no committee ever took it up; it died quietly when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Jim McDermott introduced the American Health Security Act of 2005 on March 9, 2005, with 28 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to four committees—Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform, and Armed Services—and later to the Health and Military Personnel subcommittees [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the action history ends with the subcommittee referrals in April 2005 [S5].
The bill accumulated 62 cosponsors—61 Democrats and 1 Independent—roughly 30% of the House, all from one party [S4].
The bill would have ended Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, federal employee health benefits, and CHAMPUS, and banned private insurance duplicating the new program's benefits [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health insurance industry kept its market, since the bill banning duplicative private coverage never advanced. Employers avoided the new payroll tax, and the congressional majority avoided a vote on a single-payer proposal. Americans remained under the existing mixed public-private system.

sides.party_line_note: All 62 cosponsors were Democrats (61) or the Independent (1); no Republican cosponsor is recorded, and the Republican-controlled committees that received the bill took no action on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill eliminates Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, and federal employee private coverage and bans the sale of any health insurance that duplicates the public program's benefits—wiping out the core market of the private health insurance industry. Its revenue depends on charging households premiums and cost-sharing that the public program would replace.

industries.industry: Insurance brokers and utilization review firms
industries.note: The bill eliminates utilization review programs and prohibits providers from charging patients anything beyond the program payment, removing the claims-management and pre-authorization businesses built around private coverage.

Drug coverage would be purchased by state programs at set payment rates under section 615, replacing fragmented private negotiations with government purchasing power that typically means lower prices. Manufacturers would gain universal drug coverage but lose pricing leverage.

Hospitals would be paid through approved global operating budgets—guaranteed revenue replacing uncompensated care and billing complexity, but at negotiated rates rather than private charges, and with no balance billing allowed.
Excise taxes on tobacco products would increase to help finance the trust fund, raising costs for the industry and its customers.

Employers would pay a new payroll tax and lose the ability to offer duplicative health coverage, but would shed the employee health insurance premiums they finance today—a shift in cost with an uncertain net effect.
